#2640. Arman Tsarukyan OK With Volkanovski vs. Gaethe on 1 Condition

UFC lightweight contender Arman Tsarukyan is OK with Alexander Volkanovski fighting Justin Gaethje next, on one condition.

Tsarukyan is the No. 1 contender in the UFC lightweight division to Gaethje's lightweight belt, but the organization is said to be seriously considering booking Gaethje against Volkanovski next in a superfight between champions.

Tsarukyan says that's just fine with him, but on one condition: that Gaethje vacates his belt.

Speaking to MMAFighting.com, Tsarukyan said that he's fine with Gaethje fighting Volkanovski next, but only if Gaethje gives up his belt, because Tsarukyan is tired of waiting for his long-awaited title shot.

"If Gaethje wants to fight Volkanovski, he's got to leave the belt and do like a random fight without the title because I'm the number one contender and the UFC told me that I'm fighting for the belt. I don't think they're going to do something else," Tsarukyan said (via Bloody Elbow).

With Gaethje and Volkanovski both 38 years old and nearing the end of their respective MMA careers, a superfight between these two for all the marbles does make a lot of sense, as both can walk away into the sunset afterwards.

But, as Tsarukyan said, if that's what the UFC wants to do, then he still wants to fight for the title, though it would be against someone else — potentially someone like Paddy Pimblett or Ilia Topuria.

So we will have to wait and see what the UFC wants to do with the lightweight division, and first, we need to find out what Gaethje himself wants to do, as he's been on the fence about whether or not he wants to fight again or retire from mixed martial arts.

Gaethje is coming off the best win of his career over Topuria at UFC Freedom 250, so if he retires now, he'd be walking away on top of his game. But at the same time, he'd also be leaving a lot of money on the table, which is why a Volkanovski superfight makes so much sense.

#2639. Things get physical as Spurs fan shoves Luka Doncic in wild exchange with Lakers star

The Los Angeles Lakers couldn't hold on to a 20-point lead Friday night, and Luka Doncic couldn't hold on to his temper.

Moments after the San Antonio Spurs stunned the Lakers with a 99-96 comeback victory in their NBA Cup Group C matchup, Doncic got into a heated altercation with two courtside fans that required security to intervene.

Video captured by Amazon Prime Video's postgame broadcast showed Doncic walking toward the visitors' locker room when a woman sitting courtside appeared to say something to the Lakers superstar.

Luka Doncic of the Los Angeles Lakers reacts during a game against the San Antonio Spurs in San Antonio, Texas, Friday, Nov. 27th, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

Doncic dismissively tossed his white wristband at the woman before continuing toward the tunnel. Seconds later, he doubled back to retrieve it.

Los Angeles Lakers guard Luka Doncic #77 is shoved by a Spurs' fan sitting courtside in San Antonio. Amazon Prime

The woman's male companion, who had picked up the wristband, handed it back to Doncic before shoving the five-time All-Star with his right hand as he walked away.

Doncic stopped in his tracks and turned around, but Lakers teammate Jarred Vanderbilt restrained him before leaning toward the fan and exchanging words.

Los Angeles Lakers guard Luka Doncic #77 is shoved by a Spurs' fan sitting courtside in San Antonio.

Security quickly intervened, and the male fan was subsequently ejected while Doncic retreated to the Lakers' locker room.

It's unclear what was initially said to Doncic, but throwing his wristband at a spectator was an unnecessary lapse in judgment. That, however, doesn't give a paying customer license to put his hands on an NBA player.

With the entire incident captured on camera, Doncic could face a fine or suspension from the NBA. It's unknown whether the fan will face additional punishment.

The altercation punctuated a spectacular collapse by the Lakers, whose 20-point first-half advantage evaporated like water on hot pavement. San Antonio outscored Los Angeles 30-14 in the third quarter, tying the game entering the fourth before pulling off the upset.

The Lakers lost their composure long before Doncic reached the tunnel.

#2638. MLB rumors: Yankees moves heating up, plus latest on Tarik Skubal, Mets, Padres, Red Sox, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The uncertain 2026-27 Major League Baseball offseason is fully underway. The ongoing CBA negotiations and the near-certainty of an owner-implemented lockout on Dec. 2 loom over all, and it may indeed mean a flurry of trades and free-agent signings leading up to that date. That was certainly the case leading up to the last lockout of 2021-22, and this time around we've already seen some leading examples.

Thanks to that prospect of a hastened pace, offseason rumors are flowing. Speaking of which, we'll be here each day to round up what's out there. You can find Friday's supply just below.

The buzz at the GM Meetings last week was that the Mets offered top free agent Tarik Skubal a nine-year contract worth almost $400 million, reports MLB Network Radio. If the deal is worth at least $390 million, it would set new records for total guarantee and average annual value given to a pitcher. Here are the current pitcher contract records:

Given the player and the deep-pocketed teams involved in the bidding (Blue Jays, Dodgers, Mets, etc.), Skubal is well-positioned to shatter Yamamoto's record. He could beat Scherzer's and Verlander's record as well. The expected lockout will begin after the collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1. Skubal is likely to sign before then.

The Diamondbacks are set to acquire righty Johan Oviedo from the Red Sox for minor-league lefty Luke Dotson and a player to be named later, reports the Arizona Republic. Boston had four pitchers for the No. 5 starter's spot (Oviedo, Brayan Bello, Kutter Crawford, Tanner Houck) and always seemed likely to trade one to ease the logjam.

Acquired from the Pirates last offseason, Oviedo made just one ineffective appearance around elbow trouble in 2026. He returned from Tommy John surgery in 2025 and looked excellent, and Arizona will hope Oviedo rediscovers that magic as he gets further away from his injuries. Dotson is not a top prospect. It's a low-cost flier for the D-backs.

The Tigers have signed right-hander Troy Melton to a six-year extension worth $46.5 million, reports ESPN. There is a club option for a seventh year and escalators can push the total guarantee to $80 million. Melton still had five years of team control. The new extension buys out his five team control years and one free agent year with an option for another free agent year.

Melton, 26 next month, missed the start of the season with elbow inflammation and finished the season on the injured list with more elbow woes. Between injuries, he made 20 starts with a sub-3.00 ERA with strong under-the-hood numbers. The Tigers know him better than anyone and are obviously comfortable with Melton's medicals to lock him up long-term.

The New York Yankees have agreed to a two-year contract with veteran right-hander Jonathan Loáisiga, ESPN reports. The deal also includes a club option for 2029 and is worth roughly $18 million, according to MLB.com.

Loáisiga, 32, is coming off that strong season above for the Arizona Diamondbacks, and for his career boasts an ERA+ of 128 across parts of nine MLB seasons. He's worked in relief for almost all of that span, and eight of those nine seasons came with the Yankees.

New York Yankees general manager Brian Cashman was recently asked if he'd be willing to play Spencer Jones in center field. In response, he told media, including SNY, this:

"I would be comfortable with that. At the same time Jasson Domínguez is pounding the ball in winter ball. The entire industry is noticing that based on the phone calls I'm getting."

The 23-year-old Domínguez still has big-time power potential, and defensively he's best suited to center field. For his career in the Bronx, he has an OPS+ of 93, but his 751 plate appearances have been doled out erratically across four seasons. As things stand now, he'll once again be subject to a playing-time crunch. Aaron Judge and Cody Bellinger are installed at the outfield corners, and Giancarlo Stanton, if healthy, should get much of the playing time at DH. That leaves center field for Jones or Domínguez. Other teams no doubt see that bottleneck and are seeing if Cashman and the Yankees are willing to relieve it through trade.

Lefty ace and two-time American League Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal remains far and away the top talent on the free-agent market. While the New York Mets and incumbent Los Angeles Dodgers seem like the favorites to secure his services, the San Diego Padres also have significant interest in him. That interest took the next step on Thursday with an in-person meeting, The Athletic reports. The Padres are the fourth team to meet with Skubal, who turned 30 on Friday. Previously, the Dodgers, Mets, and Toronto Blue Jays met with him.

The Padres have a pronounced need in the rotation, especially if free-agent right-hander Michael King signs elsewhere. Last winter, they also lost Dylan Cease to the Blue Jays via free agency.

The Padres and left-handed platoon hitter Gavin Sheets have agreed to a three-year, $11 million contract extension that includes two opt-outs, FanSided reports. Sheets, who'll turn 31 in April, had been slated for free agency after the upcoming season. Instead, he and the Padres will now be potentially committed through the 2029 season, depending on whether Sheets exercises any of his opt-outs. While he's not much of a hitter for average, he does draw walks and hit for power. In two seasons with San Diego, he's tallied 36 home runs and 44 doubles in 855 at-bats while seeing DH, first base, and the outfield corners.

The New York Mets have agreed to a three-year, $12 million deal with right-handed reliever Darwinzon Hernández, reports José F. Rivera.

Hernández, who turns 30 in December, hasn't pitched in MLB since 2022 and instead has revived his career with four strong seasons in Japan. Over that span for Softbank of the NPB, he's put up an ERA of 2.46 in 131 ⅔ innings with 168 strikeouts and 42 unintentional walks. Prior to rebuilding himself in Japan, Hernández had a 5.06 ERA and a 1.82 K/BB ratio over parts of four seasons with the Boston Red Sox.

#2636. No. 3 Texas at Texas A&M final score: Longhorns defense holds late in 16-6 win

A berth in the SEC championship game and a first-round by in the College Football Playoff are on the line for the No. 3 Texas Longhorns in the Lone Star Showdown against the Texas A&M Aggies on Friday in College Station.

After Texas won the toss and deferred to the second half, Texas A&M picked up one first down before punting away to the Longhorns, who went three and out, but freshman wide receiver Kohen Brown recovered the muffed punt and senior kicker Gianni Spetic connected from 54 yards when the drive stalled.

Struggling to catch kicks, the Aggies had to start their second possession on their own 7-yard line because of another muff.

Overcoming a holding penalty on first down and a delay of game penalty on third down, Texas A&M quarterback Brady Hart completed a 10-yard pass against Texas senior cornerback Bo Mascoe to move the chains, doing so again on third down when Mascoe was flagged for pass interference. Into Longhorns territory, the Aggies had a decision to make on 4th and 3 from the 40-yard line, opting to take a delay of game and punt the ball away.

Good pass protection on 3rd and 3 allowed Texas senior quarterback Arch Manning to connect with sophomore tight end Emaree Winston for a 14-yard gain, then hit junior wide receiver Emmett Mosley V for 13 yards. Snapping the ball before the end of the first quarter, Manning improvised on a shovel pass to fifth-year running back Raleek Brown for eight yards on 2nd and 9.

In 21 personnel, sophomore running back Michael Terry III took a handoff, got vertical, and ran through a tackle attempt for an 18-yard gain. Looking to score for just outside the red zone, Texas head coach Steve Sarkisian called a double pass for junior wide receiver Ryan Wingo, who made a good decision not to throw it, instead settling for a two-yard gain.

Put behind the chains when a nine-yard reception by fifth-year tight end Michael Masunas was negated by offensive pass interference, the Longhorns got into a manageable 3rd and 3 thanks to an 18-yard reception by Wingo on an free-access throw by Manning. After a lengthy injury timeout for a Texas A&M defender, a designed quarterback run for Manning moved the chains with the help of some leg drive from the Texas quarterback.

In an empty formation, Manning connected with Masunas on a short pass that gained 13 yards.

On 1st and goal from the 3-yard line, Manning's pass was tipped at the line of scrimmage, but managed to flutter its way into the strong hands of junior wide receiver Cam Coleman, who had a two-way go and ran a good slant route to score the touchdown and go up 10-0.

With former starting quarterback Marcel Reed into the game, two carries by Reed went for four yards before his departure in favor of Hart. On 3rd and 6, an easy-access throw when senior linebacker Rasheem Biles got lost in coverage resulted in a first down.

Hart misfired on a slant on 2nd and 10, forcing a more difficult conversion. A comeback to Isaiah Horton went for eight yards, but A&M head coach Mike Elko made another conservative decision to punt on 4th and 2.

Terry flashed his athleticism with a hurdle on second down to pick up eight yards and a first down, carrying it two more times for three yards and eight yards. On a toss sweep to Terry, the play got blown up by a linebacker coming downhill for a six-yard loss. After a tunnel screen to Mosley, a deep over to the Stanford transfer was delivered well by Manning under pressure, but Mosley couldn't extend to make the grab, forcing a punt.

Trying to throw the ball on first down, Hart held it too long and Texas senior edge Brad Spence beat the running back in pass protection for a sack. After sophomore nickel back Graceson Littleton broke up a screen pass on second down, Hart had to throw the ball away on 3rd and 17.

A friendly roll on the 53-yard punt by Tyler White flipped the field. Scrambling for eight yards, Manning started the drive positively, and appeared to pick up a first down with a scramble on 3rd and 10 that was negated by a holding call against senior left tackle Melvin Siani.

After Texas punted, Texas A&M mounted an effective drive highlighted by a 19-yard reception by Aaron Gregory and a pass-interference penalty on senior safety Jelani McDonald on 3rd and 3 at the edge of field-goal range. David Olano ultimately finished the half with a 52-yard field goal to make it 10-3.

The Longhorns opened the second half with an incompletion targeting Coleman, who was held at the top of his route, and a short run by Brown to set up 3rd and 9. Forced to check down to Winston, the sophomore tight end was dropped near the line of scrimmage for a three and out.

Another easy-access completion to Mario Craver on a slant initially appeared to be a positive second-down play, but Craver just lost the football turning up the field and McDonald recovered. A lengthy review upheld the call on the field and Texas took over at A&M's 34-yard line.

With the Longhorns offensive line struggling to create any creases in the running game, Brown was dropped for no gain before freshman wide receiver Jermaine Bishop Jr. caught a short pass and gained six yards. Facing 3rd and 4, Coleman won over the middle for a first down.

Throwing a screen to Wingo from a bunch formation to the field, the blocking didn't hold up and Wingo was tackled for no gain. Looking for a touchdown, Sarkisian called a wheel route for Brown, who ran a good route against man coverage and won, but Manning couldn't deliver the ball on time because of pressure in his face and sailed it too far when he could try to make the throw. Needing to convert 3rd and 10, Manning connected with Terry for a catch spotted at nine yards. When Texas A&M called timeout before Texas went for it on 4th and 1, a sneak by Manning that created a lot of movement at the line of scrimmage.

Operating with a lack of urgency under center on 1st and 10 from the 11-yard line, Manning got a delay of game penalty, then missed Coleman on a glance run-pass option and Mosley on a back-shoulder fade. Unable to get a play called in a timely manner, Texas had to burn its first timeout of the second half to run a 3rd and 15 play, a double move to Coleman that never had a chance.

The Horns had to settle for a 33-yard field goal by Spetic and a 13-3 lead.

Looking for a big play on 2nd and 4, Gregory used a double move to beat Mascoe, who had to hold to negate the explosive play. A slot fade to Gregory on 3rd and 4 beat Littleton for a 30-yard gain, and A&M was on the edge of the red zone.

Two runs by Carsyn Baker netted zero yards and Hart came under quick pressure, forcing him to throw underneath to Gregory for six yards, resulting in a 35-yard field goal to make it 13-6.

A rare kickoff return for senior Ryan Niblett was returned for 32 yards to the 35-yard line, but Brown was cut down for a one-yard gain on first down. On 2nd and 9, a comeback route for Coleman resulted in a run after the catch and an important 19-yard gain.

The drive quickly lost momentum when Brown didn't run a route as Manning expected and the Texas quarterback nearly threw an interception trying to find Mosley over the middle. A pass to Coleman was completed just short of the first down and Sarkisian decided to go for it on 4th and 1, a handoff to Terry that was stuffed in the backfield.

After a four-yard completion on first down, McDonald came downhill with aggression against the run and inflicted a tackle for loss. On 3rd and 7, senior linebacker Justin Cryer wrapped his blitz around sophomore defensive end Lance Jackson and sacked Hart for a big loss that ended the third quarter.

After A&M's punt, Texas took over at its 38-yard line, where Manning scrambled for 13 yards by identifying man coverage and taking advantage of the space that afforded him. A personal foul for going low on a Longhorns offensive lineman resulted in 15 yards for Texas. On 2nd and 7 looking for a shot play, Manning took a five-yard sack with nowhere to throw the ball. A bubble screen to Wingo picked up 19 yards behind a good block from Mosley and an escort from the offensive line.

Mosley drew a holding penalty on a pass over the middle that would have otherwise gone for a touchdown, but another pass over the middle, this time to Wingo, went incomplete. #2635. Luis Gil, Nolan Gorman, Trevor Larnach, more hit MLB free agency after non-tender deadline

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Friday marked the non-tender deadline in Major League Baseball. That important date on the offseason calendar is when clubs must make, or "tender," contract offers for the upcoming season to all their arbitration-eligible and pre-arbitration players on the 40-player roster. That's every player who isn't a free agent or isn't presently signed to a multi-year contract. Players who are tendered a contract by that deadline remain with their current organizations. Players who aren't offered a contract become free agents.

Most such decisions are easy and obvious. Others, however, present difficult calls for the organization because of roster crunches, crowded depth charts, or, more commonly, reluctance to retain a player as his salary rises through the arbitration process. While a number of non-tendered players are likely on their way out of the league, a select few others qualify as at least interesting to other teams and, on occasion, a few will even be coveted to varying degrees.

All that sets the stage for what follows, which is our list of the most compelling non-tendered players who are now on the market and available for hire. Let's get to it …

The 2024 AL Rookie of the Year, Gil has been injured and ineffective the last two seasons. He missed time with a shoulder issue this past season and also spent time in Triple-A. The Yankees moved him to the bullpen late in the season to see whether he could contribute that way, though Gil was unable to make a strong impression in that role. Now 28, Gil still has another three seasons of team control remaining. Whichever team signs him will be able to keep him through 2029, and that extra control, plus his Rookie of the Year pedigree, will no doubt land Gil with a new team before Opening Day.

As a 23-year-old in 2023, the infielder and former first-rounder hit 27 home runs in 119 games and looked like a future cornerstone for the Cardinals. Gorman, however, has gotten steadily worse since then thanks largely to his persistent strikeout issues. Last season, he wound up back at Triple-A for an extended stretch and didn't fare any better upon being recalled. Long-term, the Cardinals will likely look to hand the third base position to rising power prospect Jesús Báez, who was recently added to the 40-player roster. Gorman can be a plus at third and probably still get by at second, and no doubt some team will take a chance on his power.

On the downside, Larnach is a defensive minus at the corner outfield spots and probably needs to be a DH, and he's also a platoon bat. On the upside, he's been a steady producer from the left side of the plate. This past season, he put up a .352 OBP and an OPS+ of 120 for Minnesota. For his career, he has an OPS+ of 106 across parts of six MLB seasons. He out-hit his underlying indicators by a bit in 2026, but Larnach is still going to be an appealing part-time bat for some teams.

The Twins cut bait on a right-hander who's made 139 career starts for them since his 2021 big-league debut. Ober boasts a career OPS+ of 102, but that figure has slid over the last two seasons. What's also slid is Ober's fastball velocity, which may be why he's on this list. In his rookie season, he averaged a fringy 92.4 mph with his four-seamer, but last season that figure was down all the way to 88 mph. That put him in the very bottom percentile among MLB hurlers. The 31-year-old Ober still should draw some interest as a depth piece.

A platoon extraordinaire, Raley has always hit for power against righties, including 15 home runs in only 290 plate appearances against them in 2026. He's sneaky fast and a very good athlete for his size (6-foot-3 and 235 lbs.), good enough to handle the corner outfield spots competently. Raley also has first base experience and can patrol center field in a pinch. The Mariners cut him loose even though he will remain under team control through 2028. Raley's power against righties and an extra year of control could make him a solid bench option moving forward.

#2633. Messi's defending champions Miami knocked out of MLS Cup playoffs

Columbus Crew, with an injury-time goal from Santiago Rodriguez, beat Lionel Messi's Inter Miami 1-0 to knock the defending champions out of the first round of the MLS Cup playoffs on Friday.

Rodriguez's goal in the second minute of stoppage time gave Columbus a 2-0 triumph in the best-of-three first-round series, after their stunning 3-0 victory in game one in Florida.

Defending the MLS Cup was the last chance the ambitious franchise co-owned by David Beckham had to salvage its season after falling in the round of 16 of the CONCACAF Champions Cup and in the group stage of the Leagues Cup.

The only trophy that made it into Miami's cabinet this year was the Campeones Cup, the annual matchup between the champions of MLS and the Mexican league.

For Argentine superstar Messi, MLS's top scorer in the regular season and the favorite to win an unprecedented third straight Most Valuable Player award, it was a second first-round exit in the three MLS Cup playoffs he has contested.

In 2024 Miami stumbled against Atlanta United before earning their first MLS Cup crown last year.

The star-studded side featuring Luis Suarez, Casemiro and Rodrigo De Paul as well as Messi, had chances to score on a cold, rainy night in Ohio.

German Berterame had a golden opportunity six minutes from full time, but his header from point-blank range went over the crossbar.

"For me, the defeat is totally unfair because I think the team rose to the occasion, we deserved to win it throughout the whole match," said Miami coach Cristian "Kily" Gonzalez. "The clearest chances were ours, but that's football.

"The opponents defended well, too. Even though Leo didn't have a shot on target, we created a lot of chances."

The match appeared headed for a penalty shootout with injury time ticking away. But Inter's defense allowed Rodriguez to bring down a cross in the box from Moroccan Anass Zaroury and blast it past Canadian goalkeeper Dayne St. Clair.

Miami's early exit extends the champion's curse in MLS. No team has retained the title since the Los Angeles Galaxy in 2012.

Gonzalez shook up his starting lineup, leaving Suarez on the bench in favor of young Brazilian Riquelme Fillipi in a change that gave Miami's attack a spark in the first half.

But Messi made an uncharacteristic error in the box after a pinpoint pass from Berterame and Columbus keeper Patrick Schulte came up with a series of saves.

Columbus came close to scoring in the 65th when St. Clair saved a header from Gonzalo Tapia and Miami's Micael blocked the quick follow-up from Brais Mendez.

Gonzalez inserted Suarez with 15 minutes remaining, but Miami still couldn't capitalize on their chances. A Casemiro header was disallowed for offside and Berterame missed a header.

In the day's only other contest, Emmanuel Sabbi's 58th-minute goal lifted the Vancouver Whitecaps to a 1-0 victory over Real Salt Lake for a 2-0 sweep of their first-round series.

#2630. Mike McCarthy admits he hasn't spent enough time with the defense

After registering an unlikely 27-5 win over the previously 8-2 Broncos, Steelers coach Mike McCarthy wasn't angry, resentful, or defiant.

He was the same guy he always is, and he admitted that (as former Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers said this week), McCarthy hasn't been sufficiently invested in the side of the ball that isn't his personal expertise.

"I have not spent enough time with the defense," McCarthy told reporters. "You know, and that's something that, as far as job responsibility, job description, you know, these are things that'll be looked at in the offseason. But, you know, it's a point in our year where we're making adjustments and definitely conscientious of it. But at the end of the day, we have to all do our jobs and make sure we're giving the players the plan and all the other things that they need that we can perform and play with that type of urgency, physicality that we played today."

McCarthy prefaced his comments with a lesson he learned as a boy, growing up in Pittsburgh.

"My father used to tell me all the time as a kid, 'You tell the truth, you only have to tell your story once,'" McCarthy said.

The truth is that this week has entailed two sharply different versions of reality, where both things can indeed be the truth. One, McCarthy (like all of us) has flaws. Two, Rodgers should not have spoken about them publicly.

Rodgers clumsily defended his decision to break the code of a football locker room by texting this to Al Michaels: "The code or sanctity exists to protect the integrity of the locker room, not to provide immunity from accountability for its leadership."

That's fine, but how does disregarding the "sanctity" of the locker room (a word Rodgers undoubtedly selected in response to Tom Brady using it on Thursday) create "accountability"? McCarthy is accountable to team owner Art Rooney II. Not to the media or the fans.

And to what end? He was either doing it to help the Steelers save their season, or he was lashing out.

We'll let you decide which explanation is more likely.

#2625. Lakers blow 20-point lead in NBA Cup loss to Spurs in biggest test of season

SAN ANTONIO — JJ Redick, and the rest of the Lakers, acknowledged the four-game road trip would be a "massive challenge" because of different tests each team would present.

The biggest test of the trip, and the season so far, came Friday night at Frost Bank Center in the form of Spurs, the reigning Western Conference champions.

And for the first 19 minutes, the Lakers looked like a team ready to ace the test. But the problems they had to answer evolved, and they didn't find enough solutions, leading to the Lakers blowing a 20-point lead and suffering a 99-96 loss to the Spurs to close out NBA Cup group play.

Victor Wembanyama, who scored 25 points and grabbed 16 rebounds, celebrates during the Lakers' 99-96 NBA Cup loss to the Spurs on Nov. 27, 2026, in San Antonio. AP

The Lakers fell to 15-4 with the defeat, with the Spurs improving to 16-4 in a battle between the top two teams in the Western Conference.

And though neither Luka Dončić nor Victor Wembanyama had an efficient offensive performance, the Spurs star big man got the bragging rights, at least for one night, in the battle between two of the top contenders for MVP.

Dončić had 31 points, eight assists and six rebounds, but made just 1 of his 13 3-point attempts (14 for 31 from the field) on a night the Lakers struggled with their outside shooting — especially in the second half.

The Lakers shot 28.6% on 3s (6 of 21) in the final two quarters, with the returning Austin Reaves being the only Laker who found a consistent rhythm from beyond the arc.

Reaves (21 points, eight rebounds on 8-of-15 shooting) made all five of his 3s in the second half, including two late in the fourth to keep the game close after struggling with his ball security (seven of Lakers' 20 turnovers).

Wembanyama led the Spurs with 25 points (10-of-25 shooting) and 16 rebounds, while Stephon Castle had team-highs of 26 points and nine assists.

Luka Dončić, who scored 31 points, dribbles up court during the Lakers' 99-96 road loss to the Spurs. NBAE via Getty Images

The Lakers dominated the Spurs early, with nearly flawless execution of their defensive game plan to play off San Antonio's struggling 3-pointer shooters and shrink the floor against Wembanyama.

They held the Spurs to 38.9% shooting in the opening quarter, including 0 for 6 on 3s after the Spurs missed their final six shots (four 3s) of the first.

The Lakers' defensive intensity carried over into the second, with their stout halfcourt defense helping them take a 45-25 lead midway through the quarter before the Spurs cut their deficit to 54-38 going into halftime.

But the script flipped going into the third for the Lakers, who experienced their own offensive struggles. The Lakers scored 14 points on 6-for-24 shooting (2 for 13 on 3s) in the third, with the Spurs tying the game at 68 apiece when Keldon Johnson made a corner 3 with two seconds left in the third.

The Spurs led by as many as eight points in the fourth, but Reaves and Dončić made big shots late to keep the game close before the Spurs closed them out.

#2624. Logan Webb landing spots: Five possible destinations for Giants starting pitcher on the trading block

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Coming off a disaster of a season and with a roster badly in need of an overhaul, the Giants make sense as a team to make a trade or two this offseason. Sure enough, they are "listening to trade offers" for All-Star starting pitcher Logan Webb, per The Athletic, but they'd need a "very strong return" in order to deal him.

Webb, 30, has two years and $47 million left on his current deal. He went 8-9 with a 4.31 ERA and 1.3 WAR last season, but it was his worst year in quite a while. He averaged 4.5 WAR per season in the previous four years with a 3.22 ERA and led the National League in innings pitched from 2023 to 2025, racking up three straight top-six Cy Young finishes.

Which teams might make for a good fit for Webb? Many of them. We're talking about a workhorse under team control for two more years. Let's run through five of the best fits while, again, knowing that basically any contender should be interested in at least a conversation with the Giants.

The Cubs need so much pitching this offseason. Their entire rotation heading into the playoffs last season is in free agency. This isn't hyperbole. Matthew Boyd, Shota Imanaga, Kevin Gausman, Clay Holmes and David Peterson are all off the roster. If the Cubs were to try and put together a rotation right now, it would be something like Justin Steele, Edward Cabrera, Javier Assad and several question marks. Ben Brown and Cade Horton will open the season on the injured list.

Do we really need to spell out what a reliable innings eater would mean for this bunch? Webb is an outstanding fit here.

The upstart playoff team last season was a ton of fun, but also was running bullpen games in the ALDS. The White Sox just attached Davis Martin to Luis Castillo in a trade to the Rockies in order to offload Castillo's contract, too, so they're down a starter. The Dustin May signing means they have him along with Sean Burke and converted reliever Grant Taylor. The White Sox would reportedly like to sign another starter in the May ballpark, but what about trading for someone better like Webb?

A top four in the rotation of Webb, Burke, Taylor and May would be exponentially better than what the Sox had last season.

Returns of Spencer Strider and Spencer Schwellenbach at some point will help, but this is still a thin rotation for a team coming off a division title. Chris Sale remains, but he's followed up with Grant Holmes and Bryce Elder before the Spencers return. Youngster Didier Fuentes moving to the rotation is exciting, but there are an awful lot of questions behind Sale, who turns 38 in late March, by the way.

Given that the Padres reside in the NL West with the Giants, there might be a bit of an intradivision tax in terms of the asking price, but Padres boss A.J. Preller is never shy about offloading prospects. There could certainly be a fit. The Padres need rotation help, too, after losing Michael King, Nick Pivetta, Robbie Ray and others to free agency. We know they're in on Tarik Skubal, but that doesn't mean they'll be content with just landing one big fish.

Look at the current Padres rotation. It's basically Joe Musgrove and Randy Vásquez. With three straight playoff berths and zero trips to the World Series, now isn't the time to have Jhony Brito, Ryan Weiss and Ian Koenig make up 60% of the rotation.

Dealing for Webb and signing Skubal would make for a nice offseason for new ownership, no?

One of the most disappointing teams in baseball last season needs to have a prolific offseason. We've heard plenty about the Mets being involved in the Skubal sweepstakes and we've seen them win a monster bidding war before (see: Soto, Juan). Grabbing Webb would make it quite a well-rounded rotation with talented youngsters Nolan McLean, Christian Scott and Zac Thornton.

#2623. Jets getting much-needed defensive reinforcement with David Onyemata’s return

Three years ago, David Onyemata missed three games with an ankle injury. In 2020, the defensive tackle missed one game with a calf injury.

Those four games represented the entirety of his injury-related absences during his first 10 years in the NFL.

However, it has been nearly 10 weeks since the 33-year-old has taken the field — following core-muscle surgery — after just two appearances with the Jets.

"It's part of the business," Onyemata said. "Things like this happen. You try not to think too much about it. You just try to stay involved mentally and physically; just be present in the moment and present for the guys."

Though Onyemata is listed as questionable for Sunday's game at Miami, the veteran — who was a full participant in practice all week — told The Post that he will return to the field for the first time since Week 2.

Jets defensive lineman David Onyemata practices during training camp on Aug. 17, 2026, in Florham Park, N.J. Bill Kostroun/New York Post

"I feel great," Onyemata said. "Getting back out there, getting in the rhythm of things and being with the guys has been great."

Onyemata — who came from Atlanta on a one-year, $10.5 million deal — was a much-needed 300-pound addition, signed to help overhaul a defense that finished 29th in the league against the run in head coach Aaron Glenn's first season.

Last season, Onyemata — who played for the Saints when Glenn was a defensive coach there — ranked eighth overall and against the run, out of 127 interior defensive linemen, according to Pro Football Focus.

The Nigeria-born defender has played just 45 snaps with the Jets, who rank 30th in the league in rushing yards allowed per game (137.4) and tied for last in rushing first downs allowed per game (8.3).

"[He's] a veteran presence and someone that knows the system inside and out," Glenn said Friday. "Extremely tough, extremely violent, and there is a trust there."

Glenn's defensive line could also soon be boosted by the return of T'Vondre Sweat (knee), who was placed on injured reserve following the Week 7 loss to the Dolphins.

Jets defensive lineman David Onyemata speaks to reporters after a training practice on Aug. 17, 2026 in Florham Park, N.J. Bill Kostroun/New York Post

The 25-year-old, 366-pound defensive tackle — who was acquired from the Titans in an offseason trade for Jermaine Johnson — opened his 21-day practice window this week and was a full participant in every session since Wednesday, but he is listed as questionable.

Glenn made it clear how much it would mean for the defense to bring back the former second-round pick, who has 17 tackles and seven quarterback pressures in seven games (six starts) this season.

"When it comes to Sweat, when you build your defense, you want to build it through the middle, and he's a guy that we always felt could be that key cog in the middle of our defense," Glenn said. "Both of those guys we've talked about at length about what they bring to the table."

Their absences have been especially glaring in the past three games, as the Jets have allowed an average of 174 yards rushing on 5.6 yards per carry.

In last month's loss to the Dolphins, Ollie Gordon II ran for a season-high 103 yards and a touchdown. This weekend, Miami may lean on the running back even more, with Kyle McCord set to make his third career start at quarterback.

"I think they're doing a good job of keeping it simple and saying, 'Hey we're gonna do it this way and we're gonna beat you doing some simple things,' " Jets defensive tackle Harrison Phillips said. "They've found their rhythm running the football a little bit more … I think it's a little bit more of a hard-nosed, 'Hey, we might even be telling you what we're gonna do. Can you stop it?' "

#2622. Nikita Kucherov trade request: Five potential landing spots for the reigning NHL MVP

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

One of the greatest players in Tampa Bay Lightning history may soon be wearing a different jersey. According to Sportsnet, Nikita Kucherov has told the Lightning he won't sign a contract extension and has requested a trade.

Kucherov, a two-time Stanley Cup champion and two-time Hart Trophy winner as league MVP, is one of the best players of his era. The 33-year-old just passed the legendary Steven Stamkos for the all-time franchise lead in points and has shown no signs of slowing down.

Just last season, Kucherov posted 44 goals and 86 assists en route to his second Hart Trophy win. His underlying numbers were even better with a five-on-five goal differential of plus-38 and an expected goals share of 57.0 percent. Only a select few players can drive play from the wing like Kucherov, and that makes him a unicorn of sorts.

Kucherov is in the final year of a contract that pays him $9.5 million per season, and with the salary cap rising rapidly, he's due for a gargantuan raise next summer. It sounds like Kucherov and the Lightning were too far apart on that number, so the superstar winger has shifted his focuse to a change of scenery.

It's important to note that Kucherov has limited trade protection in the form of a 10-team trade list, but that should be more than enough for the Lightning to find a suitable trade partner. With that in mind, let's take a look at five teams that would be ideal fits for Kucherov as he prepares for the next chapter of his illustrious career.

Right out of the gate, this is the most natural fit of all the potential landing spots. General manager Kent Hughes has done a superb job of locking down his young core on team-friendly contracts, and as a result, the Canadiens have nearly $30 million in projected cap space for next season. They also have a glaring need in their top two lines, and I'd say the reigning Hart Trophy winner would fill that role quite nicely.

Montreal's moment to strike is now. It's an ascendant team with a great salary cap situtation and assets to spend. It's time to make a splash, and this would be a tsunami. Just imagine Kucherov on a power play unit with Nick Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Lane Hutson and Ivan Demidov. Kucherov would also be coached by former Lightning teammate Martin St. Louis, so a rapport would already exist between player and coach. I expect the Canadiens to do everything in their power to land Kucherov.

We already know the Wild are big-game hunting at forward because they've been heavily linked to former Detroit Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin. If I were advising general manager Bill Guerin -- and I'm certainly not -- I would recommend Minnesota package whatever assets it has offered Detroit and redirect them to Tampa Bay. No, Kucherov is not a center,  and that's the Wild's biggest need.

However, Kucherov is a rare breed of winger in that he can drive play better than most first-line centers from the wing. Put him on a line with Kirill Kaprizov, and the only time opponents will touch the puck is when they're pulling out of the net.

With Quinn Hughes also on an expiring contract, acquiring Kucherov would be a risky move for the Wild. What if they give up premium assets only to lose Kucherov and Hughes next summer? I don't think fear can dictate Minnesota's decisions. The team has a top-two defenseman in the world on its roster right now, and it has the opportunity to acquire a top-five forward. Worry about next summer when the time comes. Go all in to win the Cup while you have a chance.

It was no secret that the Hurricanes were in on the Connor Hellebuyck sweepstakes but just missed out. So, if they can't get better at preventing goals, why not get much better at scoring them? Carolina doesn't exactly need any help offensively, but adding Kucherov would go a long way to helping the team repeat as Stanley Cup champions. Besides, Kucherov would provide another level of playmaking and finishing that the Canes don't currently have on their roster.

Carolina has a good chunk of cap space available already, and it wouldn't need to shed much in order to make room for Kucherov. The Canes also have some enticing young players on their roster that might appeal to the Bolts, and they have three first-round picks over the next two drafts. Why not take a shot at landing a superstar winger?

Similar to the Hurricanes, the Mammoth were in the mix to acquire Hellebucyk, and for good reason. The goaltending tandem of Karel Vejmelka and Sebastian Cossa has not been good, so Utah may have to outscore its problems until one of the goalies finds a groove. Offense may be the best defense for the Mammoth -- and if that's the case -- then Kucherov should be in the mix for the Norris Trophy. There is a great young core of forwards in Salt Lake City, and I think Kucherov would be a perfect fit alongside Logan Cooley, who is emerging as a franchise center.

Utah also has plenty of draft capital with which to work, and it's projected for just over $25 million in salary cap space next season. The Mammoth don't have any major pending free agents on their cap sheet, so they're a suitor capable of signing Kucherov to a long-term extension.

Allow me to get a little bold on the fifth and final destination. The Stars have already failed to sign 27-year-old winger Jason Robertson to a long-term extension once. The two sides agreed to a one-year deal worth $12 million prior to the season, but Robertson's future with the team is still very much in doubt. What if Dallas and Tampa Bay executed a true "hockey trade" -- one player for one player?

Dallas would get the better player in Kucherov, but there are no guarantees regarding an extension. The Stars are in win-now mode, and Kucherov could help them get over the Cup hump immediately. Tampa Bay would get a younger player in Robertson, and although he doesn't have the elite playmaking ability of Kucherov, he's still an exceptionally talented scorer. Perhaps the Bolts could get him to join the team's core and sign a multi-year contract. This deal could work for both sides.

#2620. Lakers player grades: L.A. falls short to Spurs in NBA Cup showdown

The Los Angeles Lakers headed to Frost Bank Center to face the San Antonio Spurs in an NBA Cup group-play showdown on Friday at full strength. Austin Reaves, who had missed each of their last five games with a bruised heel, was cleared to play, and they likely felt they had a great chance of coming away with a victory.

Early on, it certainly looked like they were on their way to toppling the defending Western Conference champions. An 11-2 run in the last four minutes and change of the first quarter gave them a 27-14 lead at the end of the period, and they still led 54-38 at halftime. The Lakers held the Spurs to 42.5% shooting in the first half, and the Spurs only made two shots outside the paint during that time.

But L.A.'s offense became icy in the third quarter. The Spurs scored 13 unanswered points late in the third quarter and in the opening moments of the fourth period to go up 82-78, and then they took an 81-73 lead with 7:19 left in the fourth quarter. L.A. kept fighting, but with under a minute left, it gave up an offensive rebound off a missed free throw by Victor Wembanyama and left Stephon Castle open, allowing Castle to hit a 3-pointer for a 96-90 San Antonio advantage.

The Lakers then got a trey from Reaves and forced a double-dribble violation by De'Aaron Fox. Forward Jake LaRavia was intentionally fouled to prevent a 3-point attempt, and he made both ensuing free throws. Fox then made two foul shots after being intentionally fouled, and Quentin Grimes, after being intentionally fouled himself with 3.9 seconds to go, made his first free throw and missed the second one, resulting in a 99-96 Lakers loss.

For the game, the Lakers shot just 43% from the field and 28.6% from 3-point range, and they made just 35.6% of their overall attempts after halftime. They also gave up 13 offensive rebounds and 20 second-chance points while being outscored 17-5 in fast-break points.

They now hold a 15-4 record, while San Antonio is now tied with the Philadelphia 76ers for the NBA's best record at 16-4. As a result of Friday's loss, Los Angeles will not advance to the knockout rounds of the Emirates NBA Cup.

Thybulle helped muck things up defensively with four steals and one block in 21 minutes, but he contributed nothing offensively. He missed all four of his shot attempts, and all four of them came from beyond the arc. He went scoreless and had two rebounds and two assists.

LaRavia had a decent offensive effort by making three of his seven field-goal attempts, two of his four 3-point tries and two of his three free throw attempts to score 10 points in 34 minutes. But the Lakers needed more help from him on the boards. He got only three rebounds after coming into this game averaging 4.4 rebounds in 25.9 minutes a game.

Kessler scored 10 points on 3-of-5 shooting from the field, and he grabbed 13 rebounds, with eight of them coming on the offensive boards. He did a fairly good job of boxing out and giving Los Angeles additional shot opportunities.

He also had four assists, one block and one steal. Defensively, Kessler did a decent job on Wembanyama, who had 25 points and 16 rebounds but shot just 10-of-25 from the field.

Reaves was rusty early in this game, and he even airballed a 3-point attempt. He missed four shot attempts and had four turnovers before he made his first basket with 3:10 to go in the second quarter.

But from that point on, he mostly looked like his usual self. He ended up with 21 points on 8-of-15 overall shooting while hitting five of his nine attempts from 3-point range, and 13 of those points came in the fourth quarter to keep the Lakers' hopes alive.

Reaves, however, committed seven turnovers and had just one assist, although he was great on the boards with eight rebounds in 36 minutes.

Doncic scored 14 points in the first quarter, although he missed all six of his 3-point attempts during that time. Unfortunately, he cooled off considerably after halftime, going 3-of-9 from the field in the third quarter. He ended up 14-of-31 from the field for 31 points.

His 3-point shooting has become very concerning lately. Against San Antonio, he missed all but one of his 13 attempts from that distance, and he has now gone 13-of-64 from that distance in his last five games. He had shot 40.6% from downtown in his first 12 games of this season.

Doncic did help out in other areas on Friday, as he finished with six rebounds, eight assists and three steals.

Sexton helped spark the Lakers with nine first-half points on 4-of-5 shooting. But they could've used more firepower from him after halftime. He finished with 12 points on 5-of-10 shooting, plus four rebounds and one block, in 15 minutes.

In 26 minutes, Grimes was fairly efficient with nine points on 3-of-6 shooting and 2-of-4 from 3-point land, to go along with one assist, one steal and one block in 26 minutes. But this was a game during which L.A. needed plenty more offense from him, especially down the stretch and especially with Doncic struggling to find the basket often enough.

Williams was another player who needed to produce more than he did. He missed all three of his shot attempts and went scoreless, and he finished with two rebounds and three assists in 16 minutes.

In this game, Mamukelashvili finally made his first 3-pointer since Nov. 11 versus Milwaukee Bucks. But that was the only basket he made in five attempts. He finished with three points, four rebounds, one steal and one block in 13 minutes.

In six minutes, Vanderbilt went scoreless and had one rebound, and he had a nice contest of a Dylan Harper layup attempt in the third quarter, forcing Harper to come up well short of the rim.

Skubal, who turned 30 years of age on Nov. 20, is the No. 1 ranked talent on our list of the top 50 free agents for this offseason. Here's part of Mike Axisa's write-up:

"Excluding Yoshinobu Yamamoto, who was a special case as a Japanese star with no MLB track record, Skubal is the best starting pitcher to hit free agency since Gerrit Cole in 2019. He showed few long-lasting effects from the NanoScope elbow surgery in May and remains a capital-A Ace with terrific surface stats and under-the-hood performance indicators. Skubal brings four swing-and-miss pitches to the table (four-seamer, changeup, slider, curveball), a near MLB-best ability to limit exit velocity, and elite strike-throwing ability (MLB's third-lowest walk rate since 2023). Build an ace starter in a lab and he would look a lot like Skubal. He'll play the entire 2027 season at age 30, and given the things teams can do with pitchers these days, Skubal figures to remain a frontline starter for most of a long-term contract. He's the only true balance-of-power player available in free agency this offseason. Skubal can swing a division race and a postseason series all by himself."

Over the last three seasons, Skubal has pitched to a 2.42 ERA and an FIP of 2.48 in 546 innings spread over 88 starts. That amounts to a total WAR of 17.7 since the start of the 2024 campaign. Skubal remains foremost in the discussion for best pitcher in baseball, and this signing reflects that reality.

Since Skubal was traded to the Los Angeles Dodgers from the Detroit Tigers leading up to the 2026 deadline, he was ineligible to receive the qualifying offer from the Dodgers. As such, the Mets will not be penalized a draft pick for signing Skubal.

The nine years here aren't record-setting, as the longest pitcher contract remains the 12-year deal that Yoshinobu Yamamoto signed with the Dodgers. Yamamoto's $325 million was previously the largest contract for a pitcher -- obviously excepting Shohei Ohtani, as he's a two-way player -- so Skubal's $450 million shatters that record.

Coming off a disappointing 88-loss campaign in 2026, the Mets, big-spending owner Steve Cohen, and lead decision-maker David Stearns needed to make an offseason splash to improve their chances of a 2027 rebound and inspire a perhaps disaffected fan base. Skubal more than qualifies. He'll front a Mets rotation that also includes 25-year-old right-hander Nolan McLean, who himself has frontline long-term potential. In Queens, Skubal joins a roster that also includes the All-Star likes of Juan Soto, Francisco Lindor, and Bo Bichette.

Further, the Mets just locked up young outfielder A.J. Ewing to an eight-year, $95 million extension and we all know plenty about Soto's monster contract. The Mets now have Soto through 2039, Skubal through 2035, Ewing through 2034 and Lindor through 2031.

The rotation for the Mets right now looks something like:

Given the large outlay for Skubal here, the Mets should be all-in on improving the ballclub for the 2027 season, which means we shouldn't expect them to stop with just signing Skubal. That last spot in the rotation, as such, should be ticketed to someone else outside the organization at present, whether a free agent or a trade acquisition.

The landing of the top free agent available no doubt ramps up the pressure on Stearns and the Mets to deliver a playoff berth and a deep October run in 2027, but Skubal's presence also makes it much likely that such a feat comes to pass.

#2612. Malik Nabers a top Giants receiver without knowing ‘what’s a catch nowadays’

One of the NFL's best receivers doesn't know a catch from a non-catch.

Malik Nabers knows he makes a lot of big receptions for the Giants, but he is just as confused as every NFL fan once replay review gets involved. The 100-catch weapon is trying to figure out how in just the last six days … he lost a first-down catch, the Jaguars' Parker Washington lost a touchdown catch against the Giants, the Rams' Konata Mumpfield lost a touchdown catch, and the Chiefs' Rashee Rice lost a game-changing first down.

"When you go to the ground, the ball is going to move. It's going to move," Nabers said. "It doesn't mean that you dropped the ball. I don't know what's a catch nowadays. I guess you just have to not let the ball even touch the ground. You just have to hope it doesn't. Roll your body up so it doesn't. I guess you have to be more conscious now."

Nabers admittedly was nervous when an airborne Washington dragged both feet in the end zone as the Jaguars rallied against the Giants last week. But the ball moved as he crashed to the ground.

"When Parker made that catch, everybody was like 'Not in!'" Nabers said. "I watched that. I was like, 'No, he's in. Oh, my God.' When they called it [incomplete], I literally was like, 'What is a catch if that's not a catch?'"

Head coach John Harbaugh and tight end Isaiah Likely, who both joined Nabers in New York this season, understand Nabers' confusion on a personal level. Harbaugh's Ravens lost to the Steelers last season when a 13-yard catch was ruled incomplete because Likely didn't finish a third step before the ball was jarred loose.

Does Harbaugh know what a catch looks like?

"I thought I did," Harbaugh said. "Now it goes to replay, and I don't know. Once it goes to replay, it gets all real gray. That was the same way last year, so that hasn't changed."

Malik Nabers catches a pass in front of Antonio Johnson (6) of the Jacksonville Jaguars for a second-quarter touchdown. Getty Images

That's not going to stop the Giants from throwing the ball to Nabers, especially when he is lined up in the slot.

Nabers (65 catches for 747 yards and three drops) is averaging 14.8 air yards per target out of the slot, ranked No. 5 in the NFL among wide receivers with at least 15 slot targets, per NextGenStats. He has caught nine of 14 downfield targets (10-plus air yards) for 247 yards (No. 3) and three touchdowns (tied for No. 2).

"It's just tough to match him up in there," Harbaugh said. "He's good against zone. He's good against man. I think we've schemed some really good things up for him, and Isaiah also has been really good in the slot. It's tough to find a way to cover those guys in the slot, so we try to get them in there and get them open."

Nabers has accumulated 47 percent (353) of his receiving yards from the slot despite nearly one-third as many targets on the inside (26) as out wide (70). It seems to be the go-to way to feature Nabers in the red zone.

Parker Washington attempts to catch a pass in front of Dru Phillips during the fourth quarter of a game at MetLife Stadium on November 22, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. Getty Images

"It's a natural way to try to remove some of the cloud [coverage], some of the double-teams," Nabers said. "I still can get doubled in the slot — I still do. Putting me in the slot, motioning me … creates a better matchup — a wider split, a two-way release, giving me an opportunity to do stuff on their nickel or on their safeties or on their linebackers."

Case in point: The Giants drew up a mismatch of Nabers in the slot against Jaguars safety Antonio Johnson last week. Easy touchdown.

"The coaches spend a lot of time studying defense trying to get us open," Nabers said. "I didn't really think they were going to play that defense. Me being in the slot, I thought somebody was going to follow me or about to double me. When I got that coverage, I was like, 'Oh, it's just like practice.' And I took advantage of it."

The Giants had Wan'Dale Robinson in the slot during Nabers' first two seasons. Now, with rookie Malachi Fields and Darnell Mooney, there is more opportunity for Nabers to get creative.

"It's a credit to him," quarterbacks coach Brian Callahan said. "Not every receiver can handle that. It puts a lot of mental stress on with formations, motions, shifts, where you have to be, what route you are running. To see him able to handle that and still go out the way he played has been awesome."

#2611. Why a long-term mega deal for Tarik Skubal isn't actually all that risky

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The big prize of this free agent class, ace lefty and two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, has landed with the Mets on a nine-year, $450 million deal.

The knee-jerk reaction to a contract of this size in many corners will be that he won't possibly be "worth" that much and that such a deal would be a huge "risk" to the signing team.

Let's stop right there. I don't think it's all that risky. There's risk for the team on every contract, especially pitchers, of course, but in Skubal, the Mets are getting a surefire ace for nearly a decade.

Let's examine some of the reasons why such an enormous deal isn't actually that dangerous.

Since returning from surgery in 2023, Skubal has been absurdly good. Across his ages 26-29 seasons, he's made 103 starts and has gone 50-20 with a 2.47 ERA (169 ERA+), 0.92 WHIP and 757 strikeouts in 626 ⅓ innings. He's only walked 109, or 1.6 per nine innings. He rarely gets hit hard, he rarely gives up many runs, he strikes out a high number of hitters and rarely walks any. Simply, he's been good at everything.

The recent track record here says this is the best pitcher in baseball, at least in the long view (we could argue Paul Skenes was better in 2025 and Jacob Misiorowski was better in 2026, to name two examples, but if we looked at 2023-present, it isn't all that close).

There isn't a dropoff in the postseason, either. In eight playoff starts, Skubal has a 2.13 ERA, 0.79 WHIP and 70 strikeouts against nine unintentional walks in 50 ⅔ innings.

Also, the career workload isn't anything to be concerned about. Skubal heads to his age-30 season now with only 925 ⅓ innings in the regular season. Even counting the playoffs doesn't get Skubal to 1,000 innings at the big-league level. Let's go back to Skenes. He's only 24 years old and already has 495 career innings. Another ace? Justin Verlander had 1,553 ⅔ career innings through his age-29 season.

There just isn't a ton of tread on these Skubal tires.

We'll hear plenty of consternation about Skubal being 30 years old next season as it relates to signing a long-term deal. We'll also hear people say a deal is risky due to his injury history. He had Tommy John surgery in college, flexor tendon surgery in 2022 and arthroscopic surgery (a new procedure using a Nanoscope) in 2026.

The simple matter is that pretty much every pitcher nowadays has had some sort of surgery on his arm, notably the elbow, and we've seen pitchers time and again bounce back after elbow surgery to perform at a high level.

Skubal just did it. He only missed roughly six weeks after his procedure this past season. He came back to make 19 starts after the surgery and posted a 2.73 ERA with 141 strikeouts in 115 ⅓ innings.

I mentioned Verlander above. Skubal is a multi-time Cy Young winner, so it's acceptable to look at some of the best pitchers in baseball and how they aged into their late-30s in recent memory.

Again, Skubal will be in his age-30 season in 2027. His nine-year deal means it'll run through his age-38 season.

For those so worried about the long-term finances of the Cohen family, are you sure you're really worried that Skubal won't be productive through five, six or even all nine years of that deal? Given his track record, talent, pitching arsenal, relatively low workload given his age and how well some of the best pitchers have fared through their mid-30s, he actually seems like a great bet.

A decade ago, the common talking point was that long and huge deals for pitchers never age well. That isn't actually the case, for the most part. Here are some of the biggest pitcher contracts of all time and how they unfolded (or are unfolding).

Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Dodgers, 12 years, $325 million -- He came over from Japan for his age-25 season, so this one was a different animal. Still, it sure doesn't seem like it'll be a bad deal, does it?

Gerrit Cole, Yankees, 9 years, $324 million -- Through six years of the deal, Cole has missed a chunk of time due to Tommy John surgery. He's also won a Cy Young, finished top four in Cy Young voting three times, been worth 22.4 WAR and was the ace of an American League pennant winner.

Stephen Strasburg, Nationals, 7 years, $245 million -- Here's the bust. Strasburg was never healthy again after the 2019 World Series title run. Still, the Nationals wouldn't have that title without him.

Justin Verlander, Tigers, 10 years, $219.5 million -- This was the deal that ran from 2010-19. During this deal, Verlander won two Cy Youngs (one in the second year of the deal, one in the final year), a World Series, three pennants, 160 games and led the league in pitcher WAR three times.

Max Fried, Yankees, 8 years, $218 million -- It's only been two years, but Fried is 24-10 with a 2.83 ERA and finished fourth in AL Cy Young voting in his first year.

David Price, Red Sox, 7 years, $217 million -- He won a World Series in the third year of the contract. Overall, he was 53-26 with a 3.78 ERA (118 ERA+) through the course of the deal.

Corbin Burnes, Diamondbacks, 6 years, $210 million -- Burnes had his first year of the deal interrupted by Tommy John surgery. He had a 2.66 ERA through 11 starts prior to the injury. The jury's still out, but he heads to his age-32 season fully recovered now.

Zack Greinke, 6 years, $206.5 million -- Over the course of this deal, Greinke was 77-39 with a 3.55 ERA (125 ERA+) and 19.9 WAR. He had a fourth-place Cy Young finish in there.

CC Sabathia, 9 years, $202 million -- The Yankees won the World Series in Sabathia's first year there and he started the deal with three straight top-four Cy Young finishes. Overall, during this deal, he was 120-73 with 27.1 WAR and had five straight 200-plus inning seasons.

Max Scherzer, 7 years, $191.4 million -- During this contract, Scherzer won two Cy Youngs, a World Series title and 99 games with a 2.75 ERA. He posted 41.8 WAR. In the seven years on this deal, Scherzer finished in the top five in Cy Young voting six times, with 2020 being the outlier.

We can close with this. Some people might not care for such a measure, particularly the salary cap crowd who will be worried about the owners paying too much. Regardless, let's stick with the general belief that each individual WAR (1.0 WAR) is worth a bit over $8 million per season.

By this measure, Skubal was worth $48.4 million in 2024, $53.7 million in 2025 and $41.7 million last season. Putting aside how much less money he actually made than what he was doing on the field, and knowing everything laid out above, I'll ask a simple question:

Are you sure a 9-year, $450 million deal for this guy is a "risk?"

I think we could argue that it'll be a bargain.

#2610. Victor Wembanyama has dunked so much he hurt his hand, so he came up with a unique solution: The 'shunk'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Remember at the end of Space Jam, when Michael Jordan launched himself off of the butt of a MonStar to dunk from the half-court line? Well, imagine the exact opposite of that play. Instead of an impossibly long dunk, Thursday night's NBA action gave us an impossibly short jumper.

Let's set the stage here. The San Antonio Spurs are leading the Los Angeles Clippers by 12 points with under four minutes remaining. Victor Wembanyama is alone under the basket. He led the NBA with 71 dunks on the season to that point. Nobody else, as of the beginning of play Thursday, had reached even 50. But Wembanyama does not take this opportunity to slam down dunk No. 72, at least not intentionally. No, San Antonio's Martian with an eight-foot wingspan jumps directly in front of the basket... and flicks his wrist downward in what was seemingly a shooting motion. It swishes through the rim. Two points.

Did Wemby just... shoot it from above the rim??? 🤯😲 pic.twitter.com/1YDxy8mwy8

Officially, it will count as dunk No. 72 on the season for Wembanyama. Unofficially, as coined by Spurs broadcaster Sean Elliott, it was the first "shunk" of his season. Or, well, perhaps anyone's. It takes a perfect storm of circumstances to create a shunk: an uncommonly large basketball player, a lane open enough to ensure no defensive resistance, and perhaps rarest of all, a center disinterested in dunking.

That begs an important question: what compelled this maneuver? Well, as is so often the case, necessity was the mother of invention.

Wembanyama has a blister on his right hand. He doesn't know when exactly it came, but he knows where it came from. "It definitely came from dunking a lot," he told reporters after the game Thursday. The math here checks out. Wembanyama dunked 178 times in 64 games last season. That's around 2.8 dunks per game. Even if we discount the shunk, he's at 71 dunks through 16 games this season, or around 4.4.

Fortunately for the Spurs, Wembanyama has no plans to stop dunking, "but if I can avoid it, I would," he said after the win. The blister, according to Wembanyama, is quite painful. You'd hardly know it from watching him play. Wembanyama is averaging career-highs in points, rebounds, blocks and field goal percentage thus far this season. He is leading a 13-3 Spurs team that is tied for the NBA's best record thus far, and along with Luka Dončić, he is one of the two heavy favorites to win this season's MVP award.

If he's looking for a fringe benefit here, the "shunk" might save him from the "run and just dunk" esque criticism that Giannis Antetokounmpo recevied during his MVP pursuits. This is genuine innovation in the short-distance conversion space. Innovation is rarely in short supply in San Antonio. Earlier this week, Wembanyama threw himself multiple passes off of the backboard in a single quarter. Every time you turn on a Spurs game, there's a real chance Wembanyama does something you've never seen before, and the shunk is no exception.

#2608. Kentucky coach Mark Pope takes responsibility after Wildcats attempt illegal play in upset loss to Wichita State

An overtime game was already shaping up to be a bad night for Kentucky head coach Mark Pope. Then it got so much worse.

Facing unranked Wichita State on Friday, the Wildcats found themselves down by two with 5.4 seconds remaining in overtime. They had the ball and a chance to win, however, with Alex Wilkins inbounding the ball from their baseline after a Wichita State timeout.

Then something bizarre happened. Once Wilkins was given the ball, he passed the ball to Kentucky guard Mason Williams, who had run out of bounds on the baseline. The intention was clearly some trickery to find a soft spot in the Shockers' defense.

The result, however, was a turnover. The play was clearly illegal, with both members of the ESPN booth immediately saying, "They can't do that."

Both the Kentucky players and crowd were clearly confused for understandable reasons once the officials called the play dead. Another person stunned by the turn of events was Wichita State head coach Paul Mills, as he told reporters after the game:

"To be honest with you, we thought it was going to be Alex Wilkins going up the right side of the floor. So, when they ran the inbounds play off of a dead ball, I was like, 'That's not legal.'"

So, what happened? Pope took full responsibility for the play after the game, telling reporters that a brain fart caused him to forget the circumstances of the play:

"That's 100% on me, guys. That is 100% me. Somehow that changed to a live ball in my mind and I messed that up. It was really costly. It's a tough one to carry as a coach for sure.

When Pope says he thought the play was a live ball, he's referring to an inbounds play immediately after a made basket, which is the one kind of inbounds play in which players are allowed to run along the baseline and even pass to another player who can then inbound the ball.

In every other circumstance, including out of a timeout, the ball is fixed. The inbounder can't move, and he certainly can't give the ball to another player out of bounds.

Making the situation even more wild is that Kentucky very nearly won the game after that. Wichita State inbounded the ball, but an errant pass resulted in a steal for Ousmane N'Diaye, who then passed the ball to Milan Momcilovic for a would-be game-winner. The shot clanked away, though, giving Wichita State the win.

It was a mortifying way to lose a basketball game, before you even consider that Kentucky also blew a 14-point lead in the first half and committed even more mistakes down the stretch.

Add all that to the fact that Kentucky is now 4-3 after tying for seventh place in the SEC last season and that one of those wins was a one-point survival against Northern Arizona. For a program like Kentucky, that's more than enough to put you on the hot seat.

#2607. Winners and losers of the Tarik Skubal signing: Blue Jays, Dodgers strike out; David Stearns looks nervous

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The best player in a thin free agent class came off the board Sunday evening. Two-time Cy Young winning left-hander Tarik Skubal has agreed to a record nine-year, $450 million contract with the New York Mets. There's a $45 million signing bonus and $30 million in deferred payments. The team has not yet announced the signing but that should happen soon.

The $450 million contract shatters the previous record for a pitcher, which is Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million contract with the Dodgers, Skubal's most recent team. The $50 million average annual salary also shatters the previous record for a pitcher. That was $43.3 million for Max Scherzer and Justin Verlander during their time with the Mets.

Here now are our winners and losers from Skubal's monster contract with the Mets.

Let's start with the obvious: Skubal's a winner because he signed a massive, record-shattering contract. Sign a record deal and you're always a winner in my book. The Mets are a winner because they landed not just the best free agent on the market, but one of the game's best pitchers. Skubal is a power player who can swing a postseason race or a postseason series all by himself. There are very few players like that in the game and now the Mets have one to lead their rotation.

Boras, Skubal's agent, tends to shatter records, not beat them by just a little bit. Alex Rodriguez's contract with the Rangers is his Mona Lisa: A-Rod's $252 million contract was exactly double the largest contract in the four major North American sports leagues at the time (Kevin Garnett's $126 million deal with the Minnesota Timberwolves). Boras did it again with Skubal. He obliterated Yamamoto's total guarantee record, Scherzer's and Verlander's shared average annual value record, and also Max Fried's record deal for a lefty ($218 million). Once again, Boras won big.

We can add the Padres here too since they were one of the four teams to meet with Skubal in person this past week, though it was always hard to see San Diego beating out the Blue Jays, Dodgers, and Mets. The Dodgers reportedly held the line at a short-term, high-dollar contract similar to Kyle Tucker's deal, which put them at a disadvantage. Still, they no longer have Skubal in their rotation, and he's irreplaceable. The Blue Jays have been trying to sign top free agents for years (Tucker, Shohei Ohtani, Juan Soto, etc.) and have yet to land the plane. Point is, these teams met and pursued Skubal, then he signed elsewhere. Ergo, losers.

With Skubal off the board, the market for second- and third-tier free agent starters should quickly pick up. That group includes Michael King, Freddy Peralta, and Trevor Rogers. Skubal signing this early is a big win for everyone, really, and especially the other free agent starters. They have more than a week to negotiate and sign before the owners are expected to lock out the players after the current CBA expires at 11:59 p.m. on Dec. 1. Pitchers are coming off the board fast and furious right now. Expect that to continue for another week or so.

To be sure, the Mets' president of baseball operations is a winner because his team now employs Skubal. This is 100% a Steve Cohen contract, though. Stearns has been against long-term contracts for pitchers throughout his career as an executive, even if he said during the GM Meetings that he works on a "case-by-case basis," and it's hard to believe he'd give a pitcher with three elbow surgeries on his resume this contract. It seems likely Cohen was the one pushing this deal across the finish line, and hey, he's the owner; he can do whatever he wants. Stearns is very much against long-term deals for pitchers, though. I imagine he feels at least a wee bit nervous. Plus, he really can't afford another disaster season like 2026.

Once again, the top free agent went with a big market team. The Mets are signing Skubal this offseason. The Dodgers signed Tucker last offseason. The Mets signed Soto the offseason before that. The Dodgers signed Ohtani the offseason before that. The folks who insist baseball needs a salary cap, both the owners themselves and the fans who lean that way, now have more ammunition for their fight. Settle in. It is very, very likely we're in for months of salary cap debate during an extended lockout. That was true even before Skubal signed.
